$comment: Performance baseline for task 1.5, derived from real CI history rather than
from one machine. Every sample below came from a green ubuntu-latest job on
this branch, across Node 22 and Node 24.
These thresholds are valid ONLY on a pinned platform. The same metrics on an
unpinned machine are noise: the store slope measured CV 10.8% here against
27.6% on a contributor laptop, which is the evidence behind the
Bands are sized from the observed spread, not picked. Raising one requires
saying why in the commit; lowering one as the code improves is the point.

storeWriteMarginalMicrosecondsPerEvent.description: Least-squares slope of JsonStore.mutate() p50 against stored policy events.
storeWriteMarginalMicrosecondsPerEvent.thresholdRationale: 1.42x the highest of 22 observations (2.81) and ~5.7 standard deviations above the mean. Tightened from the initial 8.0, which was set with no history.

policyDecisionP50Microseconds.description: evaluateCommand p50 over the corpus, median of repeated sweeps.
policyDecisionP50Microseconds.thresholdRationale: 1.55x the highest of 14 observations (7.75), ~5 standard deviations above the mean. Kept comparatively loose because this metric's CV is 23.3% even on pinned CI. Tightened from 15.0.

$superseded: SUPERSEDED: every sample below was measured against the REGEX policy engine,
which main replaced with the capability engine (capabilities.ts +
shell-parse.ts). A structural shell parser is a different cost class - the
same corpus measures roughly 10x the old per-command cost - so these
thresholds no longer describe the code they gate.
The absolute assertions that used them are skipped rather than retuned by
hand. Retuning to make a build green is how a gate stops meaning anything;
the samples have to be re-collected from CI runs of the new engine, the way
these were, before an absolute can be asserted again.
The slope and linearity checks that do not depend on absolute cost still run.
